Think of GalaSwap as a vast, newly opened map with 2,000 prime plots of digital real estate. How do we get that number? Take the top ~500 most traded tokens and pair them against the four market heavyweights: BTC, ETH, USDT, and USDC.

The "Wide Open" Opportunity

Michigan Primary: Democratic Party's Hostile Takeover

Two candidates, one Senate seat, zero grown-ups in the room. Michigan Democrats spent Tuesday picking between the establishment's chosen suit and the progressive left's populist mascot — and somehow the debate over health care and genocide accusations got less airtime than a fight over who has better "authentic" vibes.

Meet the contestants: Haley Stevens, the AIPAC-backed centrist who flipped a red district once and never lets you forget it. And Abdul El-Sayed, the Bernie-and-AOC-endorsed Medicare-for-all evangelist who apparently moonlights as a debate-stage insult comic.

His pitch on Stevens: she's "a suit with a large AIPAC bank account, that's it. I hope maybe they find some way to teach her how to string together two coherent sentences." Class act.

Her comeback: she's "the only one on this stage who doesn't have a talent agent trying to pitch me for paid speeches" — followed by an X post accusing him of wanting to blame "all of your problems on Jewish Americans." Meanwhile the pro-Israel lobby quietly wired $30 million into her campaign, which is presumably just democracy doing its thing.

Then there's the accent scandal — Stevens promising to fight "with a little bit of joy, a little bit of enthusiasm, a little bit of energy and a little bit of stick it to 'em," which somehow became a bigger national conversation than either candidate's actual Gaza policy.

 El-Sayed, ever the statesman, told supporters to knock it off and focus on "things that have nothing to do with her policies or politics" — right after calling her illiterate on live television.

So here's the merger memo: one side has the AIPAC checkbook, the other has the moral high ground and a Twitter following. Both insist they're fighting for Michigan. Neither has explained how insulting each other's grammar or accent flips a swing state.


As of 12 a.m. Eastern Wednesday — three hours after polls closed — El-Sayed led 49.7 to 46.3 with about 60% counted. But his lead was built on Election Day ballots, and what's left to count is mail, which Stevens is winning by roughly the same margin he's winning the walk-ins. 

Most of it sits in Wayne County, half-tabulated, breaking eight points her way. Mallory McMorrow, who quit on July 5 and stayed on the ballot anyway, was outpolling the gap between them.

Whoever wins gets to face a Trump-backed Republican in November. Genuinely unclear which primary loss would hurt less.

Who's really running this race — the voters, or the super PACs and talent agents standing just off camera?

YOUR BANK DEPOSIT MAY SOON MOVE LIKE A TOKEN ❣️

The next major blockchain product may not look like crypto.

It may look like an ordinary corporate bank balance.

Wells Fargo reportedly plans to introduce tokenized deposits for corporate and commercial clients, initially representing US dollars and British pounds on the bank’s own blockchain infrastructure.

The first use case is expected to focus on cross-border transfers, with the ability to move funds outside conventional banking hours.

A tokenized deposit is still a claim against a bank.

But the record of that claim can become:

• transferable
• programmable
• available around the clock
• connected to automated settlement workflows

This matters because corporate money still moves through systems built around:

• banking hours
• regional cut-off times
• separate messaging networks
• manual reconciliation
• delayed settlement

Tokenization does not remove the bank.

It changes the infrastructure the bank uses.

The important distinction is that Wall Street is no longer asking whether blockchain can support payments.

Institutions are deciding which form of digital money should move through it:

⏺stablecoins

⏺tokenized bank deposits

⏺central bank money

⏺tokenized money-market instruments

The winner may not be one universal asset.

Different forms of digital money may serve different users, networks and regulatory requirements.

The future of banking may still involve deposits.
The deposit itself is becoming programmable.

Source: Wells Fargo’s reported tokenized-deposit rollout for corporate clients.

Digital money and blockchain-based settlement involve operational, liquidity, cybersecurity and counterparty risks.
